newsitem.title: USA: Alpha-Beta wants drug okay despite setback.
newsitem.headline: Alpha-Beta wants drug okay despite setback.

text.p: Alpha-Beta Technology Inc said Monday it plans to seek approval to market Betafectin to a limited group of surgery patients, despite the experimental drug's disappointing overall results in Phase III trials.

Shares of Alpha-Beta were off 4/1/8 at 6-11/16 at midday, or 38 percent, after the company announced the anti-infection drug failed to show any statistical significance in pivotal trials involving 1,177 patients. In effect, results showed no statistical difference in the incidence of infections within 30 days of surgery between those receiving the drug and those receiving placebos.

But company chief executive Spiros Jamas told Reuters he aims by late 1997 to seek permission from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration to market Betafectin to one group of patients he said clearly benefitted from the drug: those who underwent non-colorectal surgeries.

He said the group had surgeries of the stomach, pancreas, small bowel and liver -- in contrast to "colorectal procedures" involving the colon and rectum in which patients showed no statistical benefit from Betafectin.

Jamas said only 22 percent of the non-colorectal group had serious infections within 30 days of surgery, as opposed to 36 percent in the placebo group -- "a clear indication of efficacy in a significant patient population."
Jamas has scheduled a meeting with FDA officials to discuss the Phase III results, at which time he will discuss his wish to proceed with a limited PLA filing.
"We will obviously request (that) we move ahead and file a Product License Application (PLA) by year-end for Betafectin in non-colorectal surgery," Jamas said.

In parallel with the PLA filing, Jamas said he was expecting to discuss with the FDA the possibility of conducting a smaller confirmatory trial to verify the effectiveness of the drug in non-colorectal surgeries.

But Carl Gordon, a Mehta and Isaly pharmaceuticals analyst, said Alpha-Beta was likely to face tough going with the FDA because the agency is usually wary of data about subgroups in larger clinical trials.
"In general, the FDA has a problem with subgroup data because so often when you try to repeat (favorable) trial results with a subgroup they can't be repeated," he said.

"The reality is the company missed their overall end point, the main point of the trial," said Gordon, who forecast the FDA would require a confirmatory trial of the non- colorectal subgroup before seriously considering a PLA.
